## Before we start {.unnumbered}

This session uses data from previous sessions. Make sure the following files are in place:

```
intro_to_gis/
├── exercises_code/
│   └── ex_5.qmd
└── data/
    ├── raw/
    │   ├── raster/
    │   │   └── sedac_pop_2000.TIFF          <- from Session 3
    │   ├── gadm41_DEU_shp/                  <- from Session 2
    │   └── precip.mon.ltm.1991-2020.nc      <- NEW: download from OPAL
    └── tmp/
        └── january_rain.tif                 <- will be created in this session
```

The precipitation NetCDF file can also be downloaded directly from [NOAA PSL](https://downloads.psl.noaa.gov/Datasets/cmap/enh/).

```{r setup}
library(pacman)

pacman::p_load(
  ggplot2,
  dplyr,
  sf,
  raster,
  terra,
  ncdf4,
  exactextractr,
  rnaturalearth,
  rnaturalearthdata,
  ggspatial,
  cartogram,
  tmap,
  leaflet,
  mapview,
  gifski,
  geodata,
  here,
  tidyr
)

here::i_am("exercises_code/ex_5.qmd")
```

```{r load-data}
pop  <- raster(here("data", "raw", "raster", "sedac_pop_2000.TIFF"))
deu_1 <- st_read(here("data", "raw", "gadm41_DEU_shp", "gadm41_DEU_1.shp"))

# Extract population for each German Land
deu_pop <- exact_extract(pop, deu_1, fun = "mean")
deu_1$pop <- deu_pop
```

## ggplot best practices for maps

You already know `geom_sf()`. Before moving to other tools, here are a few additions that make publication-quality maps.

```{r ggplot-advanced}
# Scale bar and north arrow via ggspatial
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = deu_1, aes(fill = pop)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Pop density") +
  annotation_scale(location = "br", style = "ticks") +
  annotation_north_arrow(location = "tr", which_north = "true",
                         style = north_arrow_fancy_orienteering()) +
  labs(title = "German population density by Land") +
  theme_void()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## When to use ggplot vs tmap
`ggplot` with `geom_sf` is the best choice for most static maps, especially when the map is one panel in a larger figure. `tmap` shines for multi-panel facet maps and interactive maps, where its syntax is more concise.
:::

---

## Cartograms

A cartogram distorts the physical geography so that the area of each unit is proportional to a variable (here: population). This makes differences in the variable immediately visible at the cost of geographic accuracy.

```{r cartogram-prep}
# Cartogram requires a projected CRS
deu_1_proj <- st_transform(deu_1, "+proj=merc +a=6378137 +b=6378137")
```

```{r cartogram-types}
# Continuous cartogram: shapes are distorted but still connected
deu_cont  <- cartogram_cont(deu_1_proj, "pop", itermax = 5)

# Non-contiguous cartogram: shapes shrink/grow but keep position
deu_ncont <- cartogram_ncont(deu_1_proj, "pop")

# Dorling cartogram: shapes become circles proportional to the variable
deu_dorling <- cartogram_dorling(deu_1_proj, "pop")

p1 <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_1_proj, aes(fill = pop)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() + labs(title = "Standard map") + theme_void()

p2 <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_cont, aes(fill = pop)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() + labs(title = "Continuous cartogram") + theme_void()

p3 <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_ncont, aes(fill = pop)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() + labs(title = "Non-contiguous") + theme_void()

p4 <- ggplot() + geom_sf(data = deu_dorling, aes(fill = pop)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() + labs(title = "Dorling (circles)") + theme_void()

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Cartograms in economics
Cartograms appear in papers studying electoral geography, regional inequality, and migration flows. They are effective when there is a large variance in unit size (e.g. comparing Wyoming and California) and you want the visual to reflect population or economic weight rather than land area.
:::

## tmap -- static maps

`tmap` uses a layered grammar similar to ggplot, but is designed specifically for maps. Its syntax is consistent across vector and raster data, and it handles multi-panel and interactive maps cleanly.

### Basic polygon maps

```{r tmap-basics}
# Fill only
tm_shape(deu_1) + tm_fill()

# Borders only
tm_shape(deu_1) + tm_borders()

# Both
tm_shape(deu_1) + tm_polygons()

# Colour by a variable
tm_shape(deu_1) +
  tm_polygons(col = "pop", midpoint = 0, palette = "viridis") +
  tm_layout(title = "German population density")
```

### Colour scales and breaks

```{r tmap-scales}
# Quantile breaks: equal number of units in each bin
tm_shape(deu_1) +
  tm_polygons(col = "pop", style = "quantile", palette = "viridis")

# Custom breaks
tm_shape(deu_1) +
  tm_polygons(col = "pop", breaks = c(0, 120, 150, 215), palette = "viridis")

# Choosing palette type:
# Sequential (light to dark): for one-direction data (amounts, densities)
# Diverging: for data with a meaningful midpoint (change, residuals)
# Categorical: for unordered groups

tm_shape(deu_1) +
  tm_polygons(col = "pop", style = "pretty", palette = "viridis") +
  tm_style("col_blind") +
  tm_layout(
    title = "German population density",
    frame.lwd = 2,
    legend.position = c("left", "bottom"),
    inner.margins = 0.15
  )
```

### Combining raster and vector layers

```{r tmap-layers}
saxony <- deu_1 |> filter(VARNAME_1 == "Saxony")
saxony_wgs <- st_transform(saxony, crs = 4326)

saxony_pop <- crop(pop, saxony_wgs) |> mask(saxony_wgs)

tm_shape(saxony_pop) +
  tm_raster(palette = "viridis", title = "Pop density") +
  tm_shape(saxony) +
  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.5) +
  tm_layout(title = "Saxony population density")
```

### Multi-panel layout

```{r tmap-arrange}
bavaria <- deu_1 |> filter(VARNAME_1 == "Bavaria")
bavaria_wgs <- st_transform(bavaria, crs = 4326)
bavaria_pop <- crop(pop, bavaria_wgs) |> mask(bavaria_wgs)

map_saxony <- tm_shape(saxony_pop) +
  tm_raster(palette = "viridis") +
  tm_shape(saxony) + tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(title = "Saxony")

map_bavaria <- tm_shape(bavaria_pop) +
  tm_raster(palette = "viridis") +
  tm_shape(bavaria) + tm_borders() +
  tm_layout(title = "Bavaria")

tmap_arrange(map_saxony, map_bavaria, ncol = 2)
```

## Animated maps with tmap

We use monthly precipitation data to show how `tmap` can animate a variable over time.

```{r load-precip}
rain_nc <- nc_open(here("data", "raw", "precip.mon.ltm.1991-2020.nc"))

lon <- ncvar_get(rain_nc, "lon")
lat <- ncvar_get(rain_nc, "lat", verbose = FALSE)
rain_mean <- ncvar_get(rain_nc, "precip")

fillvalue <- ncatt_get(rain_nc, "precip", "_FillValue")
rain_mean[rain_mean == fillvalue$value] <- NA
nc_close(rain_nc)

# Build individual raster layers for each month
rain_rasters <- vector("list", 12)
for (n in 1:12) {
  slice <- rain_mean[, , n]
  rain_rasters[[n]] <- raster(
    t(slice),
    xmn = min(lon), xmx = max(lon),
    ymn = min(lat), ymx = max(lat),
    crs = CRS("+proj=longlat +ellps=WGS84 +datum=WGS84 +no_defs +towgs84=0,0,0")
  )
}

jan_rain <- rain_rasters[[1]]
writeRaster(jan_rain, here("data", "tmp", "january_rain.tif"), overwrite = TRUE)
```

```{r extract-rain}
# Extract mean monthly rain for each German Land
month_names <- c("jan", "feb", "mar", "apr", "may", "jun",
                 "jul", "aug", "sep", "oct", "nov", "dec")

for (i in 1:12) {
  deu_1[[paste0(month_names[i], "_rain")]] <- exact_extract(rain_rasters[[i]], deu_1, fun = "mean")
}

# Reshape to long format for tmap facets
rain_cols <- paste0(month_names, "_rain")
deu_long  <- tidyr::pivot_longer(deu_1, cols = all_of(rain_cols),
                                  names_to = "month", values_to = "rain")
deu_long$month <- gsub("_rain", "", deu_long$month)
deu_long$month <- factor(deu_long$month, levels = month_names)
```

```{r tmap-facets}
# Static facet grid: one panel per season (Jan, Apr, Aug, Oct)
deu_seasons <- deu_long |> filter(month %in% c("jan", "apr", "aug", "oct"))

tm_shape(deu_seasons) +
  tm_polygons(col = "rain", style = "cont", palette = "viridis", title = "Mean rain") +
  tm_facets(by = "month", ncol = 2) +
  tm_layout(legend.outside.size = 0.2)
```

```{r tmap-animation, eval=FALSE}
# Animated GIF cycling through all 12 months
rain_animation <- tm_shape(deu_long) +
  tm_polygons(col = "rain", style = "cont", palette = "viridis") +
  tm_facets(along = "month") +
  tm_layout(legend.position = c("left", "bottom"))

tmap_animation(
  rain_animation,
  filename = here("rain.gif"),
  delay = 60,
  width  = 1200,
  height = 800
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## eval=FALSE for the animation
The animation chunk is set to `eval=FALSE` because rendering 12 frames takes time. Run it manually in your console. The output is saved as `rain.gif` in your project root.
:::

## Interactive maps

### tmap in view mode

Switching `tmap` to interactive mode is a single function call.

```{r tmap-interactive}
world_map <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
  st_make_valid()

pop_world <- exact_extract(pop, world_map, fun = "mean")
world_map$pop <- pop_world

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(world_map) +
  tm_polygons(col = "pop", midpoint = 0, palette = "viridis",
              popup.vars = c("name", "pop"))
```

```{r reset-tmap-mode}
# Always reset to plot mode after interactive exploration
tmap_mode("plot")
```

### leaflet

`leaflet` gives finer control over interactive maps and is the engine underneath `tmap`'s view mode. Useful when you need custom popups, multiple base layers, or more complex interactivity.

```{r leaflet}
world_wgs <- st_transform(world_map, crs = 4326)

leaflet(data = world_wgs) |>
  addTiles() |>
  addPolygons(
    fillColor  = ~colorNumeric("viridis", pop)(pop),
    fillOpacity = 0.7,
    color      = "white",
    weight     = 0.5,
    popup      = ~paste0("<b>", name, "</b><br>Pop density: ", round(pop, 1))
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    pal      = colorNumeric("viridis", world_wgs$pop),
    values   = ~pop,
    title    = "Pop density",
    position = "bottomright"
  )
```

## Exercise -- Saxony population map with tmap
1. Extract population for each Saxony Kreis from `deu_2` (load from the shapefile used in Session 2).
2. Make a `tmap` choropleth of Saxony Kreise coloured by population density with `style = "quantile"` and a `"viridis"` palette.
3. Add a layout with a title and legend positioned at the bottom left.
4. Switch to `tmap_mode("view")` and explore the interactive version. Which Kreis is most densely populated?
5. **Bonus:** Export the static map as a PNG using `tmap_save(map, filename = "saxony_pop.png")`.
:::
